title: From Sand to Eleven Nines
description: How quartz becomes one of the purest materials industry makes, and how a pen dipped in tin led to single crystals

concepts.title: From Quartzite to Polysilicon
concepts.contentHtml:
The silicon in a processor starts as quartz, though not the sort you'd scoop up on a beach. Producers feed lumps of high-grade quartzite into a submerged arc furnace, along with carbon in the form of coal, coke and wood chips. Electrodes heat the charge to around 2,000 °C, and the carbon strips oxygen from the silica (SiO2), leaving molten metallurgical-grade silicon that is about 98 to 99 percent pure. Most of it goes into aluminum alloys and silicone chemicals, and only a small share heads toward chips.

For electronics, 99 percent is filth. Purity is counted in "nines", so 99.9999999 percent is nine nines, written 9N, or roughly one foreign atom per billion silicon atoms. Chip-grade polysilicon is typically quoted at 9N to 11N, which makes it one of the purest materials produced in bulk anywhere. To get there, the silicon has to become a liquid that can be distilled. In the Siemens process, developed at the German company in the 1950s, ground silicon reacts with hydrogen chloride to make trichlorosilane (SiHCl3), a liquid that boils at about 32 °C. Repeated distillation separates out boron, phosphorus and metals, much as a still separates alcohol from water.

The purified trichlorosilane then flows with hydrogen into a bell-jar reactor holding thin silicon rods, heated electrically to around 1,100 °C. Silicon deposits on the hot rods, which thicken over days into gray logs of polycrystalline silicon. The process eats electricity, and only a handful of companies supply the electronic grade, such as Wacker in Germany and Hemlock Semiconductor in Michigan.

concepts.title: A Pen in Molten Tin
concepts.contentHtml:
Polysilicon is pure but made of countless tiny crystals, and transistors need one unbroken lattice. The method that supplies it carries the name of Jan Czochralski, a Polish chemist working for the AEG electrical company in Berlin. The founding story is an anecdote, and its details vary between tellings. In 1916, the story goes, he was studying how fast metals crystallize when he absent-mindedly dipped his pen into a crucible of molten tin instead of his inkwell, and drew out a thin thread that proved to be a single crystal. What's documented is his 1918 paper, which presented the pulling method as a way to measure crystallization speed.

It stayed a laboratory tool for three decades. In 1948 Gordon Teal and John Little at Bell Labs began pulling germanium crystals from a melt using a seed, and Teal soon moved to silicon. Industry adopted the technique and Czochralski's name. His own life ended in disgrace. After the Second World War he was accused of collaborating with the German occupiers, and although he was cleared in August 1945, Warsaw University of Technology stripped him of his professorship. He died in 1953. In 2011 an archive document showed he had helped the Polish Home Army, and the university's senate formally rehabilitated him.

A modern puller melts polysilicon in a quartz crucible under argon, with a measured pinch of boron or phosphorus to set the electrical type. A seed crystal touches the melt and is drawn up slowly, rotating, at around a millimeter a minute. A 300 mm ingot can reach about 2 meters long and weigh several hundred kilograms. By one common estimate, about 90 percent of semiconductor devices use silicon grown this way.

concepts.title: The Crucible and the Wafer
concepts.contentHtml:
The crucible matters as much as the melt. It has to hold liquid silicon at more than 1,400 °C without poisoning it, and only very pure fused quartz will do. Much of the raw quartz for those crucibles comes from one district, the mines around Spruce Pine, North Carolina, run by Sibelco and The Quartz Corp. Estimates of the district's importance vary. Press reports in 2024 put its share of the world's high-purity quartz at 80 to 90 percent, and some authors give a similar range for crucibles. When Hurricane Helene cut the town's roads, power and water in late September 2024, both companies stopped work. Sibelco said production had restarted by October 10, and chipmakers reported enough stock to avoid disruption.

Even the best crucible slowly dissolves, so Czochralski silicon carries oxygen, around 10^18 atoms per cubic centimeter. Chipmakers turn this to use, since tiny oxygen clusters deep in a wafer trap stray metal atoms away from the transistors. Where the cleanest possible silicon is needed, as in some power devices and radiation detectors, makers use the crucible-free float-zone method instead.

The finished ingot is ground to an exact diameter, notched to mark its crystal orientation, and sliced with diamond-coated wire saws. A 300 mm wafer, the standard for advanced chips since the early 2000s, is 775 micrometers thick. Each slice is lapped, etched and polished until it's flat to within nanometers, because lithography optics focus only within a very thin band. An industry effort to move to 450 mm wafers was dropped around 2016, when the retooling looked too costly.

title: Printing With Light
description: Photolithography, from a reversed microscope in 1957 to the 193 nm immersion scanner

concepts.title: A Microscope Run Backward
concepts.contentHtml:
Every pattern on a chip is printed, much like a photograph from a negative. At Bell Labs in 1955, Jules Andrus and Walter Bond borrowed photoengraving methods from printed circuit boards to pattern silicon. In 1957 Jay Lathrop and James Nall, at the US Army's Diamond Ordnance Fuze Laboratories, went further. In the version of the story usually told, they turned a microscope's optics around, so that instead of enlarging something small it shrank a pattern onto a germanium sample coated with a light-sensitive Kodak resist. Their October 1957 patent used it to lay down thin metal strips connecting transistors. The Army gave them a $25,000 award in 1958.

The basic sequence has barely changed. A wafer is coated with photoresist, a polymer whose solubility changes where light strikes it. Light passes through a mask (called a reticle when it holds the pattern for one exposure) carrying the circuit layout in chrome on quartz. A developer then washes away either the exposed resist, in a positive resist, or the unexposed resist, in a negative one. The remaining resist is a stencil: the wafer beneath is etched or implanted only where it is gone. Then the resist is stripped and the loop repeats, dozens of times per chip.

By 1958 Jay Last and Robert Noyce at Fairchild had built a step-and-repeat camera to print many identical transistors on one wafer. Printing one field, moving the wafer and printing again is still how chips are exposed. Today's machines are scanners: reticle and wafer glide in step past a narrow slit of light, and the optics shrink the pattern four times, to a field of at most 26 by 33 millimeters.

concepts.title: The Wavelength Race
concepts.contentHtml:
A lens cannot print details much smaller than the light it uses. Lithographers sum this up in the Rayleigh criterion: the smallest printable feature equals a factor called k1, times the wavelength, divided by the numerical aperture (NA), a measure of how wide a cone of light the lens can gather. That leaves three ways to print finer lines: shorter light, wider lenses, or tricks that push k1 down toward its physical floor of 0.25 for evenly spaced lines.

For about four decades the industry mostly chose shorter light. Mercury lamps supplied the g-line at 436 nanometers, first used in high-volume manufacturing around 1982, and the i-line at 365 nm, around 1990. Then came excimer lasers: krypton fluoride at 248 nm, around 1994, and argon fluoride at 193 nm, around 2001. The next planned step, fluorine lasers at 157 nm, ran into trouble, partly because calcium fluoride lens material of the needed quality was hard to get. In May 2003 Intel dropped 157 nm from its roadmap, and TSMC canceled its orders that October.

Each new wavelength also needed a new resist, because a polymer tuned to one wavelength may absorb too much or react too little at the next. The 248 nm generation depended on chemically amplified resists, invented at IBM in the early 1980s by Hiroshi Ito, Grant Willson and Jean Fréchet, in which each absorbed photon releases an acid that triggers many further reactions. That multiplication made the resists sensitive enough for the dimmer deep ultraviolet sources. Yet features kept shrinking after 2001 while the wavelength stayed at 193 nm, through the methods in the next concept.

concepts.title: Water, Doubling and Tricks
concepts.contentHtml:
When 157 nm faltered, the TSMC engineer Burn Lin argued in 2002 for a different route: fill the gap between the last lens and the wafer with ultrapure water. Water's refractive index at 193 nm is about 1.44, against 1.0003 for air, so the lens can deliver a wider cone of light than is possible in air. Immersion pushed NA from just under 1.0 to 1.35. TSMC took delivery of an early ASML immersion scanner in 2004, and by the end of the decade 193 nm immersion, written 193i, was the industry's most-used production tool. It still prints most patterned layers of most chips made today.

Plugging in the numbers, 0.25 times 193 divided by 1.35 gives about 36 nm, and practical single exposures stop near 38 to 40 nm half-pitch for dense lines. Tighter patterns need multiple patterning. In the simplest form, two separate masks each print alternate lines. In self-aligned double patterning, a thin film is deposited on the sides of printed lines, the original lines are etched away, and the leftover sidewall "spacers" form a grid at half the original pitch. Repeating the trick, quadruple patterning, quarters it. Each extra pass adds cost and time and another chance for layers to misalign.

Masks are also distorted on purpose. Light diffracts around tiny openings, so a square drawn on a mask prints as a rounded blob. Optical proximity correction software therefore adds serifs, hammerheads and extra slivers to the mask so that the printed shape matches what the designer intended. Phase-shifting masks go further, using interference between light waves to sharpen edges.

title: EUV: The Hardest Machine
description: Tin droplets, laser pulses and near-perfect mirrors: how 13.5 nm light is made, and why one company sells it

concepts.title: Light From Exploding Tin
concepts.contentHtml:
Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light, at 13.5 nanometers, is about fourteen times shorter in wavelength than 193 nm light, and nothing produces it conveniently. ASML's machines make it by blowing up tin. A generator fires droplets of molten tin, each about 25 to 30 micrometers across, through a vacuum chamber at about 70 meters per second. A weaker laser pulse hits each droplet and flattens it into a pancake. A powerful carbon dioxide laser pulse, from amplifiers built by the German firm Trumpf, then vaporizes it into a plasma that glows in EUV. The cycle repeats about 50,000 times a second. ASML puts the temperature reached at about 500,000 kelvin; whatever the exact figure, it is many times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

Only about 5 to 6 percent of the laser energy striking the tin comes out as usable EUV. Production sources of the early 2020s delivered roughly 250 watts of it into the scanner, and the drive laser needs far more electricity than that, so a single EUV tool draws on the order of a megawatt. A curved collector mirror gathers the light, while hydrogen gas helps keep tin debris off it.

The idea is old. Hiroo Kinoshita at Japan's NTT showed early projection images at these wavelengths in the mid-1980s, to a skeptical audience. In 1997 Intel, AMD and Motorola formed EUV LLC, a consortium that agreed to pay $250 million over three years to three US national laboratories, Lawrence Livermore, Lawrence Berkeley and Sandia, for basic research. ASML bought the San Diego light-source maker Cymer in 2013, and EUV entered chip production only in 2018 and 2019, in Samsung's 7 nm and TSMC's N7+ processes.

concepts.title: Mirrors Flat to a Few Atoms
concepts.contentHtml:
Glass lenses are useless at 13.5 nm, because all matter absorbs EUV, air included. The whole light path therefore runs in vacuum, and every lens is replaced by a mirror. Even the mask is a mirror: a reflective stack with the circuit pattern written in an absorbing layer on top, rather than chrome on clear quartz.

Ordinary mirrors reflect almost no EUV, so these work by interference. Each is coated with 40 to 50 pairs of alternating molybdenum and silicon layers, each only a few nanometers thick, spaced so that the faint reflections from every interface add up in step. The best stacks reflect about 70 percent at 13.5 nm. With around ten reflections between source and wafer, only a few percent of the light survives the trip, one reason the source must be so bright.

The mirrors come from Carl Zeiss SMT in Oberkochen, Germany. Zeiss's favorite comparison is that if one of its EUV mirrors were blown up to the size of Germany, its largest deviation from the ideal shape would be about 0.1 millimeter. The newest High-NA systems raise the numerical aperture from 0.33 to 0.55, at the cost of halving the exposure field, so the largest chips must be stitched together from two exposures.

Short light brings its own problem. Each EUV photon carries about 92 electron volts, roughly fourteen times the energy of a 193 nm photon, so the same dose arrives as far fewer photons. At the scale of one tiny contact hole the count is small enough for chance to matter, and a few holes in many millions may print missing or merged. These random, or stochastic, defects often set the practical limit.

concepts.title: One Supplier, Forty Containers
concepts.contentHtml:
ASML, based in Veldhoven in the Netherlands, was founded in 1984 as a joint venture of Philips and ASM International. It is the only company that sells EUV scanners; Nikon and Canon, its old rivals in earlier lithography tools, never brought EUV to market. By one 2025 estimate ASML took about 83 percent of the world's lithography equipment sales.

A standard EUV scanner is roughly the size of a bus, weighs about 180 metric tons and contains around 100,000 parts. ASML says shipping one takes about 40 freight containers, 20 trucks and three cargo planes, and installing it at a fab takes months. In 2023 ASML recognized 9.1 billion euros of revenue on 53 EUV systems, an average of roughly 170 million euros each. The first High-NA machine, the EXE:5000, began shipping to Intel's site in Oregon in December 2023; press estimates of its price in 2024 ranged from about 300 to 400 million dollars.

Behind the scanner stands a narrow pyramid of suppliers: Zeiss for optics, Trumpf for lasers, Cymer for the source and hundreds of specialist firms below them. That concentration turned EUV into an instrument of policy. SMIC, China's largest chipmaker, ordered an EUV scanner in 2018, but in 2019 the Dutch export license for it lapsed and was not renewed. Press reports blamed US pressure; ASML said only that it needed a valid license. As of 2026, ASML states that it has never delivered an EUV system to China.

title: Building a Transistor in Layers
description: Doping, etching and deposition, the move from flat transistors to fins and nanosheets, and why "3 nm" measures nothing

concepts.title: Spoiling Silicon on Purpose
concepts.contentHtml:
After all the effort to reach eleven nines, the first thing a fab does is contaminate the silicon deliberately. Pure silicon conducts poorly. A few atoms of phosphorus or arsenic, each with one more outer electron than silicon, make it n-type, rich in free electrons; boron, with one fewer, makes it p-type, rich in "holes." A transistor is a pattern of such regions.

Early fabs baked wafers in furnaces filled with dopant vapor and let the atoms diffuse in. Most doping today uses ion implantation: dopant atoms are ionized, accelerated by an electric field and fired into the wafer, with the energy setting how deep they go and the beam current setting how many arrive. The impacts knock silicon atoms out of place, so the wafer is then annealed, heated for seconds or less, sometimes with lasers or flash lamps, to repair the lattice without letting the dopants spread.

Silicon displaced germanium, the first transistor material, largely because of its oxide. In 1955 Carl Frosch and Lincoln Derick at Bell Labs accidentally grew a layer of silicon dioxide on a wafer and found that it protected the surface and blocked dopants. Germanium's oxide is unstable and dissolves in water. At Fairchild, Jean Hoerni built on the Bell work with his planar process (patent filed in 1959), which kept junctions sealed under oxide, and Robert Noyce added metal wiring on top to make a monolithic integrated circuit. At Bell Labs, Mohamed Atalla and Dawon Kahng used thin oxide as the gate insulator of the first working MOSFET, shown in 1960, ancestor of nearly every transistor made today.

concepts.title: Add, Remove, Flatten, Repeat
concepts.contentHtml:
A chip is built like a layer cake that gets carved after every layer. Deposition adds material: chemical vapor deposition grows films from reacting gases, sputtering knocks metal atoms off a target onto the wafer, and atomic layer deposition builds the thinnest films one atomic layer at a time. Etching takes material away. Wet etches, such as hydrofluoric acid dissolving oxide, eat in every direction and undercut the resist. Plasma etching, also called reactive ion etching, drives ions straight down with an electric field, so it can cut vertical walls and deep, narrow holes.

After many steps the surface turns lumpy, and the next lithography step cannot keep it all in focus. Chemical mechanical polishing (CMP), developed at IBM in the 1980s, grinds the wafer flat with a slurry and a rotating pad, an industrial version of sanding a tabletop. CMP also made possible the copper wiring IBM announced in 1997. Copper conducts better than aluminum but is hard to etch, so trenches are etched into insulator instead, filled with copper, and the excess polished away. The method is called damascene, after the inlaid metalwork associated with Damascus.

The transistors occupy only the bottom of the chip. Above them sits a stack of a dozen or more wiring levels, finest at the bottom and thickest at the top. By common industry estimates, a leading-edge wafer passes through more than a thousand individual steps of coating, exposure, etching, implantation, deposition, polishing and inspection, and spends roughly three months in the fab.

concepts.title: Fins, Nanosheets and the Fictional Nanometer
concepts.contentHtml:
A MOSFET is a switch: voltage on the gate opens or closes a channel between source and drain. For about fifty years that channel lay flat in the wafer surface, with the gate on top. As gates shrank to a few tens of nanometers, the gate lost control of the channel's depths, and current leaked even when the switch was off, wasting power as heat.

The fix was to stand the channel up. In the FinFET, the channel is a thin vertical fin and the gate drapes over three sides. Hitachi built an early version, called DELTA, in 1989, and a University of California, Berkeley group including Chenming Hu, Tsu-Jae King Liu and Jeffrey Bokor, funded by DARPA from 1997, developed it and coined "FinFET" in 2000. Intel shipped it first, in its 22 nm "tri-gate" chips of 2012, and the foundries followed at 14 and 16 nm by 2015. The next design, gate-all-around, stacks thin horizontal nanosheets and wraps the gate around every one. Samsung began 3 nm production with it in June 2022, and TSMC's N2 and Intel's 18A followed in 2025.

Node names have come loose from physics. Into the 1990s, a node name roughly matched a real dimension such as gate length. Since then it has become a generation label. TSMC's "3 nm" process has a contacted gate pitch, the spacing from one transistor's gate to the next, of about 45 nm, and its tightest metal lines sit about 23 nm apart. In 2021 Intel renamed its own nodes, calling its 10 nm-class process "Intel 7" to line up with rivals' labels. The number now corresponds to no particular dimension on the chip.

title: Cleanrooms, Yield and Thirst
description: Why fabs filter air harder than hospitals, how one speck kills a chip, and what a fab drinks and burns

concepts.title: Mr. Clean's Airflow
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1960 Willis Whitfield, a physicist at Sandia National Laboratories in New Mexico, drew up plans that changed how clean rooms worked. Earlier rooms filtered their air, but it swirled unpredictably, so dust stirred up by workers drifted around and settled anywhere. Whitfield's design flushed the room with a constant, uniform flow of highly filtered air that swept particles away before they could land. It spread quickly through industry and medicine, and Time magazine called him "Mr. Clean." Every chip fab descends from it.

Cleanliness is graded by the ISO 14644-1 classes, which count particles per cubic meter of air. Typical city air holds about 35 million particles of 0.5 micrometer or larger in each cubic meter, roughly class ISO 9. An ISO 5 room allows 3,520 such particles, and ISO 1 allows just 10 particles of 0.1 micrometer or larger. Fab bays are commonly run around ISO 5 to 7, but the wafers themselves rarely meet that air. They travel in sealed pods called FOUPs (front-opening unified pods), carried along overhead tracks by robots and opened only inside tool enclosures kept far cleaner than the room. The room air is kept at slightly higher pressure than the outside, so leaks flow out rather than in.

People remain the biggest source of dirt, shedding skin flakes, hair and droplets. Workers enter through airlocks, sometimes with air showers, wearing hooded coveralls, masks, gloves and boots, and paper and pencils are usually banned because they shed fibers. Lithography bays glow yellow, because filters remove the blue and ultraviolet light that would expose the photoresist.

concepts.title: One Speck, One Dead Chip
concepts.contentHtml:
A 300 mm wafer holds hundreds of chips, and yield, the fraction that work, decides whether a fab makes money. Many failures come from defects scattered at random: a particle, a scratch, a void in a copper line, a tiny pattern that failed to print. One "killer" defect in the wrong spot ruins the die it lands on.

The simplest model treats defects like raindrops falling at random. If a process has on average D killer defects per square centimeter and a die covers A square centimeters, the chance that a die escapes them all is e raised to the power of minus D times A. At 0.1 defects per square centimeter, a 1 square centimeter phone chip yields about 90 percent. A die of about 8 square centimeters, the size of Nvidia's H100 AI accelerator, yields only about 45 percent. Big chips are punished exponentially. Real fabs use gentler versions of the formula, because defects cluster, so large dies fare somewhat better than this simple model predicts.

Chipmakers fight back in three ways. They hunt defects, inspecting wafers with optical and electron-beam tools and tracing failures back to a machine or step; yields on a new process usually climb over months or years, and Intel's 10 nm process, planned for 2016, reached volume only in 2019 after long yield trouble. They sell imperfect chips as cheaper models with faulty cores switched off, a practice called binning. And they split large designs into several smaller dies, or chiplets, packaged together. AMD's Zen 2 processors of 2019 did this, so that one defect costs a small die rather than a whole processor.

concepts.title: What a Fab Drinks and Burns
concepts.contentHtml:
A fab is a chemical plant built around some of the cleanest water on Earth. Wafers are rinsed between many steps in ultrapure water, filtered, deionized and degassed until its electrical resistivity reaches about 18.2 megohm-centimeters, the theoretical limit for pure water at 25 °C. Tap water would leave ions and particles that wreck transistors. A large fab uses millions of liters a day, and modern plants recycle much of it.

That thirst made news in 2021, when Taiwan suffered its worst drought in more than half a century. The government rationed water in parts of the island, and water was trucked in to keep chip plants running. Fabs are also hungry for power. By one estimate TSMC alone used about 5 percent of Taiwan's electricity around 2020, more than the capital, Taipei, and a single EUV scanner draws on the order of a megawatt.

Then come the capital bills. A leading-edge fab costs tens of billions of dollars: in April 2024 TSMC raised its planned investment in Arizona to more than 65 billion dollars for three fabs. Equipment makes up most of that cost and is typically written off over about five years, so fabs run around the clock, every day of the year, to earn it back. Fabs also consume a long list of specialty gases and chemicals, from hydrofluoric acid to high-purity neon for the excimer lasers, each with its own supply chain. The steep cost is a large part of why the number of companies at the leading edge has shrunk to a few.

title: Moore's Law and the Chip Wars
description: A 1965 forecast that became a schedule, the foundry that makes most advanced chips, and chips as statecraft

concepts.title: Moore's 1965 Guess
concepts.contentHtml:
In April 1965 the trade magazine Electronics published "Cramming more components onto integrated circuits," by Gordon Moore, then research director at Fairchild Semiconductor. Moore noticed that the number of components on a chip, at the lowest cost per component, had been doubling about every year. He projected that pace ten years ahead, to as many as 65,000 components on a chip by 1975. Fifty years later he called it "a wild extrapolation."

It held well enough, and in 1975, by then a co-founder of Intel, Moore revised it to a doubling about every two years. The Caltech professor Carver Mead popularized the name "Moore's law." The often-quoted 18 months came from the Intel executive David House and referred to chip performance, not transistor count. It was never a law of nature. From the 1990s, industry roadmaps turned it into a schedule that toolmakers, chipmakers and designers all planned around, so it partly fulfilled itself.

A hidden bonus ran out first. In 1974 Robert Dennard at IBM showed that as transistors shrank, voltage and current could shrink with them, keeping power per area constant while speed rose. Leakage broke this Dennard scaling in the mid-2000s; clock speeds stalled at a few gigahertz, and chips added cores instead. Transistor counts kept climbing, but more slowly and expensively. At the end of 2023 Intel's chief executive, Pat Gelsinger, put the doubling "closer to every three years," while Nvidia's Jensen Huang had declared the law dead in 2022. Moore died in March 2023.

concepts.title: Morris Chang's Foundry
concepts.contentHtml:
For decades every serious chip company owned its own fabs. Morris Chang, who spent 25 years at Texas Instruments before moving to Taiwan in 1985 to head the government's Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI), bet on a different model. On February 21, 1987, he founded the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, with backing from the Taiwanese government and from Philips, which took a stake of about 27.5 percent and transferred technology. TSMC would design no chips of its own; it would only make chips for others. It was the first dedicated, or "pure-play," foundry.

The model freed designers from owning fabs. "Fabless" companies such as Nvidia and Qualcomm, and Apple's chip teams, send designs to a foundry; AMD spun off its own fabs as GlobalFoundries in 2009. As each new node grew more expensive, fewer firms could keep up. GlobalFoundries halted its 7 nm work in 2018, and the leading edge narrowed to three makers: TSMC, Samsung and Intel. By market-research estimates, TSMC held about two-thirds of the world's foundry revenue at the end of 2024 and about 70 percent in 2025.

A 2021 report by the Boston Consulting Group and the Semiconductor Industry Association found that 92 percent of the world's manufacturing capacity below 10 nm was in Taiwan and the other 8 percent in South Korea. That concentration underlies the idea of a "silicon shield": the argument that the world's dependence on Taiwan's fabs deters an attack on the island. The idea is debated. Critics such as Matthew Pottinger, a former US deputy national security adviser, argue that it assumes Beijing will weigh economic costs the way democracies do.

concepts.title: Chips as Statecraft
concepts.contentHtml:
The economic historian Chris Miller's Chip War (2022), which won the Financial Times Business Book of the Year award, argued that the chip supply chain, concentrated in a few firms and places, has become a central arena of rivalry between the United States and China. He noted that China spends more on imported chips than on imported oil.

On October 7, 2022, the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security issued sweeping export controls. They restricted sales to China of the most advanced AI chips and of key chipmaking tools, required licenses for equipment going to Chinese fabs making logic chips at 16 or 14 nm and below, DRAM at 18 nm half-pitch or less, or NAND flash with 128 or more layers, and required US persons to get licenses before supporting such fabs. The Netherlands and Japan announced their own equipment restrictions in 2023, and the US widened its rules in October 2023 and December 2024. At home, the CHIPS and Science Act, signed in August 2022, set aside 52.7 billion dollars for US chipmaking and research, including 39 billion in manufacturing incentives; TSMC's Arizona project was awarded up to 6.6 billion dollars in 2024.

Controls slow rather than stop. In late August 2023, while US Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo was visiting China, Huawei launched the Mate 60 Pro phone. Its Kirin 9000S chip was made by SMIC on a 7 nm-class process, which analysts concluded had been reached without EUV, apparently by multiple patterning on older deep ultraviolet scanners, a route expected to be costlier and lower-yielding. China also answered in kind, restricting exports of gallium and germanium, chipmaking metals it dominates, from August 2023.
